questions.title: Default deny with an allow rule
questions.text:
In namespace `prod` create a NetworkPolicy named `default-deny` that denies **all ingress and egress** traffic for every pod in the namespace.

Then add NetworkPolicies so that pods labelled `app=web` can still reach pods labelled `app=db` on TCP port `6379` — and nothing else can. The pod `scanner` must not be able to reach `db`.
questions.solution:
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
    kind: NetworkPolicy
    metadata:
      name: default-deny
      namespace: prod
    spec:
      podSelector: {}
      policyTypes:
      - Ingress
      - Egress
    ---
    apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
    kind: NetworkPolicy
    metadata:
      name: allow-web-to-db
      namespace: prod
    spec:
      podSelector:
        matchLabels:
          app: db
      policyTypes:
      - Ingress
      ingress:
      - from:
        - podSelector:
            matchLabels:
              app: web
        ports:
        - protocol: TCP
          port: 6379
    ---
    apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
    kind: NetworkPolicy
    metadata:
      name: allow-web-egress
      namespace: prod
    spec:
      podSelector:
        matchLabels:
          app: web
      policyTypes:
      - Egress
      egress:
      - to:
        - podSelector:
            matchLabels:
              app: db
        ports:
        - protocol: TCP
          port: 6379

Policies are additive: once `default-deny` selects a pod, only traffic some policy explicitly allows gets through. Because the deny covers egress too, `web` needs its own egress allowance to `db` (and, in a real cluster, a DNS allowance to kube-system).

checks.name: default-deny
checks.hint: default-deny must select all pods ({}) with policyTypes Ingress and Egress
web must still reach db on 6379 (allow both db ingress and web egress)
scanner must not reach db

questions.title: Ingress with TLS
questions.text:
A certificate and key for `web.prod.local` are on the base host at `/opt/tls/tls.crt` and `/opt/tls/tls.key`.

In namespace `prod` create a TLS Secret named `web-tls` from them, then an Ingress named `web-ingress` that serves host `web.prod.local` over TLS with that secret, routing `/` (Prefix) to Service `web` port `80`.
questions.solution:
kubectl -n prod create secret tls web-tls --cert=/opt/tls/tls.crt --key=/opt/tls/tls.key
    kubectl -n prod create ingress web-ingress --rule="web.prod.local/*=web:80,tls=web-tls"
    kubectl -n prod get ingress web-ingress -o yaml

The `,tls=web-tls` suffix in the rule adds `spec.tls[].secretName`. A TLS Secret has type `kubernetes.io/tls` with the keys `tls.crt` and `tls.key`.

checks.name: web-tls
checks.hint: secret web-tls must be of type kubernetes.io/tls

checks.name: web-ingress
checks.hint: web-ingress must use tls secret web-tls for web.prod.local and route to service web:80

questions.title: CIS benchmark remediation
questions.text:
Run `kube-bench` on the control plane node `cks-control` and fix every check about the `--profiling` argument: the API server, controller manager and scheduler must all run with `--profiling=false`.

Re-run `kube-bench` to confirm those checks pass and that the control plane is still healthy.
questions.solution:
ssh cks-control
    sudo -i
    kube-bench                                # [FAIL] 1.2.16, 1.3.2, 1.4.1 (profiling)
    vim /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml            # add: - --profiling=false
    vim /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-controller-manager.yaml   # add: - --profiling=false
    vim /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-scheduler.yaml            # add: - --profiling=false
    kube-bench --check 1.2.16,1.3.2,1.4.1     # PASS
    exit; exit
    kubectl -n kube-system get pods           # control plane pods Running

Each flag goes into the `command:` list of the static pod manifest; the kubelet restarts the component when the file changes. Make one change at a time and confirm `kubectl get nodes` still works after each.

checks.hint: kube-apiserver manifest lacks --profiling=false
kube-controller-manager manifest lacks --profiling=false
kube-scheduler manifest lacks --profiling=false
kube-apiserver manifest is broken
kube-controller-manager manifest is broken
kube-scheduler manifest is broken

questions.title: Least-privilege RBAC
questions.text:
The ServiceAccount `app-sa` in namespace `web` is bound to `cluster-admin` through the ClusterRoleBinding `app-sa-admin`.

Remove that binding. Instead, create a Role `pod-reader` in `web` that permits only `get` and `list` on `pods`, and a RoleBinding `app-sa-pods` binding it to `app-sa`. The ServiceAccount must not be able to delete deployments or list secrets.
questions.solution:
kubectl get clusterrolebinding app-sa-admin -o yaml     # confirm what it grants
    kubectl delete clusterrolebinding app-sa-admin
    kubectl -n web create role pod-reader --verb=get,list --resource=pods
    kubectl -n web create rolebinding app-sa-pods --role=pod-reader --serviceaccount=web:app-sa
    kubectl -n web auth can-i list pods --as=system:serviceaccount:web:app-sa        # yes
    kubectl -n web auth can-i delete deployments --as=system:serviceaccount:web:app-sa # no

Audit existing bindings with `kubectl get clusterrolebindings -o wide` and `kubectl get rolebindings -A -o wide`; anything binding `cluster-admin` to a workload identity is a finding.

checks.name: app-sa-admin
checks.hint: clusterrolebinding app-sa-admin still exists
app-sa must be able to list pods in web
app-sa must be able to get pods in web
app-sa must not be able to delete deployments
app-sa must not be able to list secrets

questions.title: Do not mount service account tokens
questions.text:
The Deployment `worker` in namespace `web` runs as ServiceAccount `worker-sa` but never talks to the API.

Disable automatic mounting of the service account token both on the ServiceAccount `worker-sa` and in the Deployment's pod template. The Deployment must remain available.
questions.solution:
kubectl -n web patch serviceaccount worker-sa -p '{"automountServiceAccountToken": false}'
    kubectl -n web patch deployment worker -p '{"spec":{"template":{"spec":{"automountServiceAccountToken": false}}}}'
    kubectl -n web rollout status deployment worker
    kubectl -n web get pod -l app=worker -o yaml | grep -A3 volumeMounts   # no kube-api-access mount

`kubectl edit` works too. Setting it on the pod spec wins over the ServiceAccount setting, so set both for defense in depth.

references.title: Configure Service Accounts for Pods — opt out of token automounting

checks.name: worker-sa
checks.hint: serviceaccount worker-sa must set automountServiceAccountToken: false

checks.name: worker
checks.hint: deployment worker pod template must set automountServiceAccountToken: false

checks.name: worker
checks.hint: deployment worker is not available

questions.title: Harden the API server
questions.text:
On the control plane node `cks-control`, the API server currently runs with `--authorization-mode=AlwaysAllow` and permits anonymous requests.

Change the static pod manifest so that authorization mode is `Node,RBAC` and anonymous authentication is disabled. The API server must come back healthy.
questions.solution:
ssh cks-control
    sudo -i
    vim /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml
      # - --authorization-mode=AlwaysAllow   ->   - --authorization-mode=Node,RBAC
      # add:  - --anonymous-auth=false
    exit; exit
    kubectl get nodes      # works again once the kubelet restarts the static pod

A typo in a flag leaves the API server crash-looping; if `kubectl` stops answering, go back to the node and check `crictl ps -a` / `journalctl -u kubelet`.

checks.hint: kube-apiserver must run with --authorization-mode=Node,RBAC
kube-apiserver must run with --anonymous-auth=false
the kube-apiserver manifest is broken

questions.title: Harden the kubelet
questions.text:
The kubelet on node `cks-node1` accepts anonymous requests and uses `AlwaysAllow` authorization.

Fix its configuration (`/var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml`) so that anonymous authentication is disabled and authorization mode is `Webhook`, then restart the kubelet. The node must stay `Ready`.
questions.solution:
ssh cks-node1
    sudo -i
    vim /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml
      # authentication.anonymous.enabled: false
      # authorization.mode: Webhook
    systemctl restart kubelet
    systemctl status kubelet
    exit; exit
    kubectl get nodes

These two settings are the kubelet equivalents of the API server's `--anonymous-auth` and `--authorization-mode`; with `AlwaysAllow`, anyone who can reach port 10250 can run commands in every container on the node.

checks.hint: kubelet config must set authentication.anonymous.enabled: false
kubelet config must set authorization.mode: Webhook

checks.name: kubelet
checks.hint: kubelet on cks-node1 is not running
cks-node1 is not Ready

questions.title: AppArmor
questions.text:
An AppArmor profile file `/etc/apparmor.d/k8s-deny-write` exists on node `cks-node1` but is not loaded.

Load it into the kernel on that node. Then create a Pod named `locked` in namespace `default` (image `busybox:1.36`, command `sleep 3600`) that runs **on `cks-node1`** with that profile applied to its container using the `securityContext.appArmorProfile` field.
questions.solution:
ssh cks-node1
    sudo apparmor_parser -q /etc/apparmor.d/k8s-deny-write
    sudo aa-status | grep k8s-deny-write
    exit

    apiVersion: v1
    kind: Pod
    metadata:
      name: locked
    spec:
      nodeName: cks-node1
      containers:
      - name: main
        image: busybox:1.36
        command: ["sleep", "3600"]
        securityContext:
          appArmorProfile:
            type: Localhost
            localhostProfile: k8s-deny-write

Profiles live on the node, not in the cluster, so the pod must be pinned to a node where the profile is loaded. Since v1.30 the field replaces the old `container.apparmor.security.beta.kubernetes.io/<name>` annotation.

references.title: Restrict a Container's Access to Resources with AppArmor

checks.hint: profile k8s-deny-write is not loaded on cks-node1 (apparmor_parser)

checks.name: locked
checks.hint: pod locked must set securityContext.appArmorProfile Localhost/k8s-deny-write on its container

checks.name: locked
checks.hint: pod locked must run on cks-node1

questions.title: seccomp profile
questions.text:
A seccomp profile is installed on every worker node at `/var/lib/kubelet/seccomp/profiles/audit.json`.

Create a Pod named `audited` in namespace `default` (image `busybox:1.36`, command `sleep 3600`) whose **pod-level** securityContext uses that Localhost seccomp profile.
questions.solution:
apiVersion: v1
    kind: Pod
    metadata:
      name: audited
    spec:
      securityContext:
        seccompProfile:
          type: Localhost
          localhostProfile: profiles/audit.json
      containers:
      - name: main
        image: busybox:1.36
        command: ["sleep", "3600"]

`localhostProfile` is relative to the kubelet's seccomp root (`/var/lib/kubelet/seccomp`). `type: RuntimeDefault` is the usual choice when no custom profile is required.

references.title: Restrict a Container's Syscalls with seccomp

checks.name: audited
checks.hint: pod audited must use pod-level seccompProfile Localhost profiles/audit.json

checks.name: audited
checks.hint: pod audited is not running

questions.title: Pod Security Admission
questions.text:
Enforce the `restricted` Pod Security Standard on namespace `restricted-ns` using Pod Security Admission labels.

The Deployment `secure-app` in that namespace violates the standard. Fix its pod template so that new pods are admitted and the Deployment becomes fully available (do not delete the Deployment).
questions.solution:
kubectl label namespace restricted-ns pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=restricted
    kubectl -n restricted-ns rollout restart deployment secure-app   # new pods are rejected: see events
    kubectl -n restricted-ns get events | grep FailedCreate
    kubectl -n restricted-ns edit deployment secure-app

A compliant container security context:

    securityContext:
      allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
      runAsNonRoot: true
      capabilities:
        drop: ["ALL"]
      seccompProfile:
        type: RuntimeDefault

and remove `privileged: true`. The restricted profile forbids privileged containers, privilege escalation, running as root, added capabilities, host namespaces and hostPath volumes. Existing pods keep running; only new pods are admitted or rejected, so the fix shows up in the new ReplicaSet.

checks.name: restricted-ns
checks.hint: namespace restricted-ns must carry pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=restricted

checks.name: secure-app
checks.hint: secure-app container must drop ALL capabilities, disallow privilege escalation and not be privileged

checks.name: secure-app
checks.hint: secure-app pods are not all available (are new pods being admitted?)

questions.title: Secrets as read-only files
questions.text: The Secret `db-creds` exists in namespace `web`. Create a Pod named `vault-client` in `web` (image `busybox:1.36`, command `sleep 3600`) that mounts the Secret as a **read-only volume** at `/etc/creds` — not as environment variables.
questions.solution:
apiVersion: v1
    kind: Pod
    metadata:
      name: vault-client
      namespace: web
    spec:
      volumes:
      - name: creds
        secret:
          secretName: db-creds
      containers:
      - name: main
        image: busybox:1.36
        command: ["sleep", "3600"]
        volumeMounts:
        - name: creds
          mountPath: /etc/creds
          readOnly: true

Verify with `kubectl -n web exec vault-client -- ls /etc/creds`. Files are updated when the Secret changes; environment variables are not, and they leak into `kubectl describe` and process listings.

checks.name: vault-client
checks.hint: vault-client must mount secret db-creds read-only at /etc/creds

checks.name: vault-client
checks.hint: pod vault-client is not running

questions.title: Sandboxed runtime
questions.text:
The nodes have gVisor installed with the runtime handler `runsc`.

Create a RuntimeClass named `gvisor` for that handler, and a Pod named `sandboxed` in namespace `default` (image `nginx:1.27`) that runs with it.
questions.solution:
apiVersion: node.k8s.io/v1
    kind: RuntimeClass
    metadata:
      name: gvisor
    handler: runsc
    ---
    apiVersion: v1
    kind: Pod
    metadata:
      name: sandboxed
    spec:
      runtimeClassName: gvisor
      containers:
      - name: nginx
        image: nginx:1.27

A RuntimeClass maps a name to a CRI handler configured on the nodes; `runtimeClassName` on the pod selects it.

checks.name: gvisor
checks.hint: runtimeclass gvisor with handler runsc missing

checks.name: sandboxed
checks.hint: pod sandboxed must set runtimeClassName: gvisor

checks.name: sandboxed
checks.hint: pod sandboxed is not running

questions.title: Scan images and remove the vulnerable ones
questions.text: Namespace `apps` has several Deployments. Using `trivy`, scan the image of each Deployment and **delete every Deployment whose image has one or more CRITICAL vulnerabilities**. Leave the others untouched.
questions.solution:
kubectl -n apps get deployments -o wide          # images
    trivy image --severity CRITICAL nginx:1.27
    trivy image --severity CRITICAL docker.io/legacy/app:2.3    # CRITICAL: 3
    trivy image --severity CRITICAL redis:7.2
    trivy image --severity CRITICAL docker.io/vendor/tool:1.0    # CRITICAL: 1
    trivy image --severity CRITICAL docker.io/acme/chat:4.1
    kubectl -n apps delete deployment beta delta

`--severity` narrows the report; the `Total:` line is the quick read. A loop saves time: `for i in $(kubectl -n apps get deploy -o jsonpath='{.items[*].spec.template.spec.containers[0].image}'); do echo $i; trivy image -s CRITICAL $i | grep Total; done` (loops are not simulated here — scan them one by one).

checks.hint: beta (docker.io/legacy/app:2.3, 3 CRITICAL) must be deleted

checks.name: delta
checks.hint: delta (docker.io/vendor/tool:1.0, 1 CRITICAL) must be deleted

checks.name: alpha
checks.hint: alpha has no CRITICAL findings and must stay

checks.name: gamma
checks.hint: gamma has no CRITICAL findings and must stay

checks.name: chatter
checks.hint: chatter has no CRITICAL findings and must stay

questions.title: Static analysis with kubesec
questions.text:
The manifest `~/hardened-pod.yaml` on the base host defines Pod `hardened`. `kubesec scan` reports a critical finding.

Fix the manifest so that kubesec reports no critical issues and the container runs as non-root with a read-only root filesystem and all capabilities dropped, then create the Pod in namespace `default`.
questions.solution:
kubesec scan ~/hardened-pod.yaml           # critical: Privileged
    vim ~/hardened-pod.yaml

    apiVersion: v1
    kind: Pod
    metadata:
      name: hardened
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: app
        image: nginx:1.27
        securityContext:
          runAsNonRoot: true
          readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
          allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
          capabilities:
            drop: ["ALL"]

    kubesec scan ~/hardened-pod.yaml           # Passed
    kubectl apply -f ~/hardened-pod.yaml

kubesec scores a manifest: `privileged`, `hostNetwork` and `hostPID` are negative critical points; non-root, read-only filesystem, dropped capabilities, resource limits and a dedicated ServiceAccount add points.

checks.name: hardened
checks.hint: pod hardened must not be privileged and must set runAsNonRoot, readOnlyRootFilesystem and drop ALL capabilities

checks.name: hardened
checks.hint: pod hardened is not running

questions.title: Enable audit logging
questions.text:
Enable API server audit logging on `cks-control`:

- write an audit policy to `/etc/kubernetes/audit-policy.yaml` that logs **Secrets** at the `Metadata` level and everything else at `RequestResponse`
- configure the API server with `--audit-policy-file=/etc/kubernetes/audit-policy.yaml`, `--audit-log-path=/var/log/kubernetes/audit/audit.log`, `--audit-log-maxage=30` and `--audit-log-maxbackup=10`

The API server must stay healthy.
questions.solution:
ssh cks-control
    sudo -i
    vim /etc/kubernetes/audit-policy.yaml

    apiVersion: audit.k8s.io/v1
    kind: Policy
    rules:
    - level: Metadata
      resources:
      - group: ""
        resources: ["secrets"]
    - level: RequestResponse

    mkdir -p /var/log/kubernetes/audit
    vim /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml
      # add to command:
      #   - --audit-policy-file=/etc/kubernetes/audit-policy.yaml
      #   - --audit-log-path=/var/log/kubernetes/audit/audit.log
      #   - --audit-log-maxage=30
      #   - --audit-log-maxbackup=10
      # and mount both paths (hostPath volumes + volumeMounts) so the static pod can read the policy and write the log

Rules are evaluated in order; the first match wins, so the Secrets rule must come before the catch-all. The policy file is read by the API server *container*, which is why it must be mounted into the pod.

checks.hint: /etc/kubernetes/audit-policy.yaml must exist and have a rule for secrets
the secrets rule must use level Metadata
kube-apiserver needs --audit-policy-file=/etc/kubernetes/audit-policy.yaml
kube-apiserver needs --audit-log-path=/var/log/kubernetes/audit/audit.log
kube-apiserver needs --audit-log-maxage=30
kube-apiserver needs --audit-log-maxbackup=10
the kube-apiserver manifest is broken

questions.title: Runtime detection with Falco
questions.text:
Falco runs on node `cks-node2` and has been reporting `Terminal shell in container` events for a workload in namespace `apps`.

Using the Falco output on that node (`journalctl -u falco` or `/var/log/falco/falco.log`), identify which Deployment the offending container belongs to and scale that Deployment to `0` replicas.
questions.solution:
ssh cks-node2
    sudo journalctl -u falco --no-pager | grep 'Terminal shell'
    # ... k8s.ns=apps k8s.pod=chatter-... image=docker.io/acme/chat:4.1 ...
    exit
    kubectl -n apps get deployments -o wide      # which deployment runs docker.io/acme/chat:4.1
    kubectl -n apps scale deployment chatter --replicas=0

Falco events name the namespace, pod and image; the pod name prefix (before the ReplicaSet hash) and the image both point at the Deployment.

checks.name: chatter
checks.hint: deployment chatter (image docker.io/acme/chat:4.1) must be scaled to 0

questions.title: Immutable containers
questions.text: Make the containers of Deployment `ledger` in namespace `web` immutable: set `readOnlyRootFilesystem: true` on the container and provide an `emptyDir` volume mounted at `/tmp` so the application can still write temporary files. The Deployment must remain fully available.
questions.solution:
kubectl -n web edit deployment ledger

    spec:
      template:
        spec:
          volumes:
          - name: tmp
            emptyDir: {}
          containers:
          - name: main
            image: nginx:1.27
            securityContext:
              readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
            volumeMounts:
            - name: tmp
              mountPath: /tmp

    kubectl -n web rollout status deployment ledger

A read-only root filesystem blocks attackers from dropping binaries into the container; writable scratch space moves to explicit volumes (`/tmp`, cache directories). Real nginx also needs writable `/var/cache/nginx` and `/var/run` — in a real cluster mount emptyDirs there too.

checks.name: ledger
checks.hint: ledger must set readOnlyRootFilesystem: true and mount an emptyDir at /tmp

checks.name: ledger
checks.hint: deployment ledger is not fully available
